articles/hacoo-express-vs-standard-shipp.title: Hacoo Express Shipping vs Standard: How to Check the Fee and ETA
articles/hacoo-express-vs-standard-shipp.intro: Compare the delivery fee, arrival dates and processing time for the same Hacoo basket. See how to decide whether an express upgrade covers your deadline.
sections: Where can I see the express price for my order?

Open the checkout for the items you intend to buy, enter the delivery destination and look at the shipping choices before authorising payment. If both standard and express appear, write down the fee and the arrival estimate for each. Subtract the standard fee from the express fee to find the price of upgrading. Then compare the last day of each delivery window with the day you actually need the parcel.

A shared screenshot can show somebody else's options without telling you what your order qualifies for. Even your own screenshot from an earlier basket leaves a question if you have since added a second item, changed a size or selected a different address. Start with the current order summary. If you found an item through this site's external catalogue, check which service runs the checkout before applying any Hacoo delivery information.
Which dates does Hacoo publish for my destination?

Hacoo's public Shipping & Delivery page gives estimated receiving times of 15–25 days for the UK, France, Germany and Italy, and 15–30 days for Spain. It groups other destinations under a much wider 25–65-day range. The range for Spain is therefore the relevant starting point for a Madrid delivery, even if the product came from a creator in France. Confirm that the actual address can be selected before relying on a published range.

The European help centre also gives a broad 15–28-day estimate and separates preparation, international movement and final delivery. Those figures describe how an order travels. They do not give you a personal delivery date, an express surcharge or a timetable for your chosen product. Use the public pages for context and keep the order-specific estimate alongside them. If the checkout gives dates, copy those dates exactly rather than reconstructing them from several general help articles.
Does express include the time before dispatch?

Read the words immediately beside the estimate. There is a practical difference between an item expected to arrive on Friday and an item expected to dispatch on Friday. For the former, compare Friday with your deadline. For the latter, you still need an estimate for the journey from dispatch to your address. A promised dispatch day by itself cannot tell you whether you will have the item for a weekend trip.

Hacoo's public shipping page describes normal processing as 3–5 business days and gives 5–7 workdays as its fastest express shipping example. It describes receiving time separately. Do not present that fastest example as a delivery promise starting the moment you pay. When the checkout already displays an arrival window that includes preparation, adding processing again would count the same stage twice. If it shows only transit time and your date is important, ask what starts that clock before purchasing.
Compare the same basket and the final amounts

Choose one destination, currency, quantity, colour and size. Record the item subtotal, delivery line, discount, any separately displayed charges and final amount. Switch just the shipping service, then record those fields again. Start over if the switch changes the selected product or the address. A useful comparison answers a narrow question: what changes when this particular parcel travels by a different service?

Here is a made-up example in euros. Suppose a €32 basket shows standard shipping at €4.50 and express at €10.50, with everything else identical. The two totals are €36.50 and €42.50, so the upgrade costs €6. These numbers illustrate the calculation only. If a discount disappears after the switch, calculate the difference between the new final totals as well. The shipping line tells you how the service is priced, while the final total tells you the extra amount you would pay.
Is the upgrade worth it for a fixed date?

Continue the example with fictional dates rather than the platform's general estimates. Suppose standard shows 18–23 June, express shows 15–19 June and you leave early on 20 June. The €6 upgrade moves the end of the displayed window ahead of departure. You would be buying a more suitable estimate, while keeping a backup in case the parcel is late. If the event is on 16 June, both windows still extend beyond it.

Try the same comparison for a flexible purchase. If you can use the item in July and both services show June arrival, ask whether having it earlier is worth the difference to you. If both display the same arrival range, look for a stated benefit you can actually use. A service name alone cannot establish that your order will reach you sooner. Also check the unit: five business days and five calendar days cover different stretches around a weekend.
What if express disappears or only one method is shown?

First confirm the delivery country, postcode and exact items. A captured price from another country gives you no basis to budget for an option missing from your checkout. If the upgrade matters, return to the basket and check the individual item for a preparation or preorder note. You can inspect a one-item basket to see which option is displayed, then restore the original selection and confirm its total before making a decision.

Hacoo's shipping information says available items and preordered or backordered items can be sent separately. If your basket contains a gift and an accessory, check whether the dates refer to both pieces. Ask which parcel a displayed estimate applies to if this is unclear. If you consider separate orders, compare the complete price of each, including their delivery charges. Splitting a basket just to reproduce an express quote can cost more than the original upgrade.

A postcode typo is worth correcting before another comparison. A parcel sent quickly to the wrong address will still miss you. If you discover an address error after paying, contact the order's support channel promptly with the order reference and ask whether the address can still be corrected.
Keep the information that will settle a later question

Before paying, keep the date of the quote, the destination, the shipping service, its fee, the expected arrival range and the final total. After payment, check the confirmation against those notes. If the confirmation gives a different estimate, record both and their dates. This gives support a specific question to investigate. When sharing an image outside the order's official support channel, crop out your name, full address and payment details.

Once the order has a shipment number, use that number to follow the journey. The product ID helps you locate the listing again; the order reference identifies the purchase; the shipment number identifies the parcel. With a split order, save which items belong to which shipment. A scan for a parcel containing your accessory cannot establish where the gift is. Check the most recent carrier event and its date before concluding that the entire order is late.
What to ask if an express delivery misses its estimate

Find the arrival range from the confirmation and the most recent tracking event. A useful support request can be this short: I chose express for this order. The confirmation showed delivery by 19 June. The last carrier scan was on 17 June, and the parcel has not arrived. Please confirm the current delivery estimate and the next step for this shipment. Add the real references privately and replace the illustrative dates with your own.

If the question is about the fee, ask separately whether the order is eligible for a review of the express charge. Keep the answer with your order record. For a parcel marked delivered, use the carrier and order-support details for that shipment rather than continuing to compare estimated dates. For an order you have yet to place, the decision still rests on two figures you can check yourself: the extra total and the latest acceptable arrival date.
takeaways: Compare the same basket, address and currency.
Save the checkout total and both delivery windows.

articles/hacoo-kids-size-guide.title: Hacoo Kids’ Sizes: How to Check Clothing and Shoe Measurements
articles/hacoo-kids-size-guide.intro: Check whether a Hacoo listing offers children's sizes, compare a garment with its chart, and measure both feet before choosing a shoe option.
sections: Does this listing actually offer a children's size?

Open the exact product, choose the colour or style you want, then inspect the available size options and their chart. Look for a children's range, a stated height or measurements that describe the selected item. A photo of a child wearing the design does not establish which sizes a seller offers today. If the listing supplies only an adult chart, look for clarification before treating the smallest adult option as a children's size.

Use a saved spreadsheet entry or product link to find the item, then make the size decision on the current listing. Write down its product identifier, colour, style and size exactly as shown. This matters on a family-matching design, where a child and an adult may wear similar-looking garments in the same photograph. If you follow an external catalogue link, take note of the destination and use the measurements published for the option you would actually buy.
Start by identifying what the chart measures

A children's clothing chart can give body measurements, finished garment measurements or both. A body chart might specify the chest circumference of the person a size is intended to fit. A finished garment chart might describe the sweatshirt laid flat. Look for the label, unit and a diagram showing the tape position. A number headed simply “chest” is ambiguous until you know whether it describes width across the front or the distance all the way around.

Keep the two comparisons separate. Use a child's measurements with a body chart and a similar piece of clothing with a finished garment chart. A sweatshirt worn over a T-shirt needs room to move, so its finished circumference and the child's chest circumference serve different purposes. If the chart cites height alone, it can help narrow the options. It still leaves open whether the sleeves are long enough or the waistband matches the trousers that fit at home.
Measure a garment that already fits well

Pick a piece the child wears comfortably in the same way. A thin school jumper gives a more useful reference for another school jumper than a thick coat does. Fasten any closure the child normally closes, lay the garment on a level surface and smooth the fabric gently. Keep a tape measure in centimetres and position its zero mark at the seam or edge pictured in the seller's diagram. Leave the fabric and elastic relaxed unless the chart asks for a stretched measurement.

For a top, note the width from underarm to underarm and the length from the indicated shoulder point to the hem. For sleeves, check where the measurement begins. A sleeve measured from the neckline includes distance that a shoulder-seam measurement leaves out. For trousers, compare the relaxed waistband, inside leg and rise when the seller provides them. Write the method beside each number. A note that says “waistband across, relaxed” will still make sense when you return to the listing a week later.
A sweatshirt example: 41 cm flat versus 82 cm around

Imagine a favourite sweatshirt measures 41 cm across the chest when laid flat. For a simple, symmetrical sweatshirt that is approximately 82 cm around at that level. Use 41 cm against a seller's flat-width column. Use roughly 82 cm only if the chart expressly measures the finished garment around its chest. It would be a mistake to describe the child as having an 82 cm chest based on this garment measurement.

Suppose two example options list flat chest widths of 40 cm and 43 cm. Compared with the 41 cm sweatshirt, one is 1 cm narrower across, and the other is 2 cm wider across. Neither number tells you the sleeve length. Compare the other dimensions and think about the intended layer. If the wider option has sleeves much longer than the reference sweatshirt, another cut may suit the child better. These example measurements explain a comparison and do not correspond to any published Hacoo size.
Measure both feet for children's shoes

Have the child wear the kind of socks they expect to use with the shoes. Put paper on a hard floor, keep it from slipping and have the child stand comfortably with weight on both feet. Mark the heel and the tip of the longest toe, keeping the pencil upright. The longest toe can be the second toe. Measure the heel-to-toe distance, repeat for the other foot and record both values in the same unit.

For example, suppose one foot measures 20.0 cm and the other measures 20.3 cm. Start from 20.3 cm when reading a chart labelled for foot length. In a millimetre chart, use 203 mm. If you repeat the measurement and get a surprising result, check the paper position, pencil angle and tape before choosing a size. Nike's children's footwear guide illustrates a similar way of measuring both feet. Use its measuring technique with the listing's own chart; its model-specific shoe sizes apply to Nike products.
Check whether the shoe chart means foot, insole or sole

A recommended foot length describes the wearer. An insole length describes part of the shoe. An outsole length includes material outside the space available to the foot. These can all be printed in centimetres and still answer different questions. With the 20.3 cm example, compare against a row expressly marked for that foot length. A photograph of a ruler next to a 20.3 cm outsole cannot establish that the child's foot will fit inside.

When a seller lists only a removable insole length, ask which foot-length range the seller recommends for the exact model and size. If you compare a removable insole from a shoe that fits, measure it using the same endpoints as the seller and mark it as an insole comparison. Width, toe-box shape, fastening and socks can all affect the fit. Avoid guessing a fixed amount of growth room or turning a child's current EU, UK or US label into a size for an unrelated shoe.
What if the measurements point to different sizes?

Start with the dimension that would cause the most trouble for that particular item. A jacket that will be zipped over layers needs enough room through the chest and shoulders. Trousers need a usable waist and enough leg length. A two-piece set can fit at the top and still be too short at the ankle. Make a separate comparison for each piece, then see whether the seller allows different sizes or offers the pieces separately.

Ask one question the seller can answer without guessing how you want the item to fit. For example: for the navy children's sweatshirt in the size marked 140, is the listed chest measurement taken flat from underarm to underarm, and what is the sleeve length from the shoulder seam? For shoes, give the longer foot measurement and ask which row on that model's chart applies. If the answer refers to a different style or colour, request the matching chart before committing.
Save the selected size and check it on arrival

Once you have chosen, keep the size chart, selected variant and the date of the check together. Review the option again in the basket because returning to a listing can change the selected colour or size. A useful note might say “navy sweatshirt, size 140, width measured flat, sleeve from shoulder”, followed by the seller's figures. Keep the child's measurements in a private note; a public review can explain the garment's measurements without naming or photographing the child.

On arrival, compare the label and selected option before removing tags or washing the garment. Lay it out and repeat the measurements using the same start and end points. For shoes, check both shoes and let the child try them on indoors with the intended socks. If something differs from the order, keep a photograph of the label and the relevant measurement and consult the order's after-sales instructions. This record helps distinguish an incorrect variant, a measurement discrepancy and a size that simply feels different in wear.
takeaways: Confirm a children’s size on the exact option.
Compare like measurements and use the larger foot.
